FunctionGemma inference,
from Mac to Raspberry Pi

A 270M-parameter model learned to complete assignment tasks through tools. The LoRA checkpoint completed 95/100 tasks on the Mac and 97/100 on an 8 GB Raspberry Pi 5. The base model completed 0/100, and Luna completed 100/100.

100 paired cases per system · 17 November 2026

Baseline, fine-tuning and the Luna benchmark

Each task asks the model to inspect a three-person roster, update the requested assignments and commit the result. A pass requires the exact intended final state and a successful explicit commit.

The base model often ended early. Its shorter task times and lower call counts include incomplete attempts.

Task completion time

The Pi averaged 36.84 seconds per task, compared with 8.59 seconds for the same merged checkpoint on the Mac, a 4.3× task-time ratio. Among the Pi's 97 successful attempts, the average was 36.64 seconds.

First-token latency on the Pi

The Pi's first model request averaged 1.39 seconds to its first generated token. Across all 299 model requests, the average was 2.07 seconds. The server returned each HTTP response after generation completed.

The on-disk checkpoint was 1,022.7 MiB. At the end of the run the server used zero swap, and the firmware reported zero throttling flags. The highest temperature sampled after a task was 56.8 °C.

How the comparison was measured

LoRA refers to a rank-16 adapter with approximately 3.8 million trainable parameters, trained using approximately 5,000 successful task demonstrations generated by GPT Luna and merged into FunctionGemma for inference.

All four systems used the same 100 frozen cases, seeds 1001–1100, with the same starting rosters, tool schemas and scoring. Each system ran one attempt per case. FunctionGemma used a 256-token output cap and greedy decoding. The Pi harness and inference server both ran locally, with a fresh SQLite database per task and a separate warm-up task excluded from its reported timings.

The Mac FunctionGemma runs used BF16 CPU inference. The Pi used FP32 CPU inference with four threads on a Raspberry Pi 5 Model B with 8 GB RAM. Both used PyTorch 2.9.1 and Transformers 4.57.6. The Pi result used the identical merged step-1884 checkpoint from the Mac's 5,000-task evaluation. The precision and hardware differences limit conclusions about the two-point completion-rate difference.

The Pi used a 60-second request deadline. A 12-case pilot with the original 30-second deadline recorded four timeouts whose generations completed in 37.5–39.1 seconds. All four assignments passed with the longer deadline. The final Pi run had zero request timeouts and three incorrect-state commits. The Mac runs used a 30-second deadline.

Luna ran through a hosted API, with a 4,096-token output cap and up to four concurrent tasks in the original cohort. Its task times include network and service overhead. FunctionGemma ran one task at a time. Hosted model memory and Mac first-token timings were unavailable in the archived measurements.

The 100 cases are disjoint from training and validation examples. They had already been examined when designing the expanded dataset, so these results describe a repeat benchmark. The separately reserved 600 final test cases were unevaluated in these runs. The expanded training run combined more data, different task proportions and additional training steps.

Measurement definitions and source records

Task time runs from process launch through exit, including SQLite and local HTTP. First-token time runs from server-side prompt formatting to the first generated token ID. P95 uses nearest rank. GNU time measured each harness process's maximum RSS. Linux process files measured server RSS and its lifetime high-water mark. Tensor storage counted shared parameter storage once.
